topic: Uses and applications of electromagnetic waves
subject: physics

items.q: Which of these correctly pairs an application with the type of electromagnetic wave used?
items.correct: Fibre optic communications – visible light
items.misconception: Satellite communications – radio waves
items.why: Radio waves are firmly linked with long-distance broadcasting, and ‘furthest’ sounds like the property needed to reach a satellite. Students also hear ‘radio signal’ used loosely for any transmitted signal. The specification pairs satellite communications with microwaves. Long-wavelength radio waves are reflected by the ionosphere, so they do not reach a satellite at all; microwaves pass through the atmosphere and the ionosphere with little absorption, so they can travel up and back down.
items.random_wrong: Cooking food in a toaster – microwaves

items.q: Which type of electromagnetic wave carries a television broadcast to a rooftop aerial?
items.correct: Radio waves
items.misconception: Microwaves
items.why: The names ‘radio wave’ and ‘radio programme’ look like a matched pair, so television seems to need a different wave, and satellite television being real makes microwaves the obvious guess. The specification pairs radio waves with both television and radio. A broadcast picked up by a rooftop aerial arrives as radio waves. Microwaves are used for the satellite link when television is delivered by satellite, but that is the satellite communications application, not the broadcast to the aerial.

items.q: Which of these is an application of microwaves?
items.correct: Sending a signal up to a satellite
items.misconception: Toasting a slice of bread in a grill
items.why: The specification pairs microwaves with cooking food, and the microwave oven is the appliance students know by name, so ‘cooking’ and ‘microwaves’ become fixed together. The specification pairs cooking food with microwaves and with infrared, because different appliances use different parts of the spectrum. A grill, toaster or radiant heater emits infrared, which is absorbed by the surface of the food and browns it. Only a microwave oven cooks with microwaves.
items.random_wrong: Sending broadband down a glass fibre

items.q: Which statement about cooking food in a microwave oven is correct?
items.correct: The microwaves are absorbed by the food and transfer energy to it.
items.misconception: The microwaves make the food itself slightly radioactive as it cooks.
items.why: The word ‘radiation’ is used both for electromagnetic waves and for the emissions from radioactive substances, and news stories about radioactivity attach the word to danger. ‘Microwave radiation’ then sounds like the same thing as nuclear radiation. Microwaves sit in the low-frequency half of the spectrum and are not ionising. They are absorbed by the food, transfer energy to it and warm it; nothing about the food is changed into a radioactive substance. Only the far end of the spectrum – ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays – is ionising, and even those do not make an object radioactive here.
items.random_wrong: The microwaves heat the middle of the food long before the outside.

items.q: A rescue team uses an infrared camera to find a person in a dark building. How does the camera form its image?
items.correct: It detects the infrared radiation emitted by the person and the room.
items.misconception: It shines a beam of infrared out and photographs what it lights up.
items.why: Every camera a student has used needs light, and the flash on a phone reinforces the idea that a camera provides its own illumination. ‘Infrared’ is then imagined as invisible torchlight. Objects emit infrared radiation themselves, and hotter objects emit more of it. An infrared camera is a detector: it collects the infrared coming from the scene and converts it into an image, which is why it works in complete darkness and shows how hot different parts of the scene are.
items.random_wrong: It detects the warm air that has risen from the person's body.

items.q: Which statement about the waves used to cook food is correct?
items.correct: A grill cooks with infrared and a microwave oven cooks with microwaves.
items.misconception: A grill, a toaster and a microwave oven all cook their food using microwaves.
items.why: The specification pairs microwaves with cooking food, and the microwave oven is the appliance students know by name, so ‘cooking’ and ‘microwaves’ become fixed together. The specification pairs cooking food with microwaves and with infrared, because different appliances use different parts of the spectrum. A grill, toaster or radiant heater emits infrared, which is absorbed by the surface of the food and browns it. Only a microwave oven cooks with microwaves.
items.random_wrong: Infrared and microwaves are simply two different names for the same wave.

items.q: Which statement about fibre optic communications is correct?
items.correct: Information travels along the glass fibre as pulses of visible light.
items.misconception: Information travels along the fibre as pulses of electric current.
items.why: Every other cable in the house carries electricity, and the word ‘cable’ itself implies a wire, so a fibre is pictured as a very thin metal conductor. The fibre is glass, not metal, and it carries no current. A transmitter turns the information into pulses of visible light, the light is reflected from the walls of the fibre so it stays inside all the way along, and a detector at the far end turns the pulses back into an electrical signal.
items.random_wrong: Information is beamed through the air as microwaves, like wi-fi.

items.q: An energy efficient fluorescent lamp produces ultraviolet inside its tube. What mainly leaves the lamp and lights the room?
items.correct: Visible light, produced by the coating on the inside of the tube.
items.misconception: Ultraviolet, since that is exactly what the lamp is designed to produce.
items.why: The specification pairs ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps, so students reasonably assume the ultraviolet is what leaves the lamp. Warnings about ultraviolet then make the lamp sound dangerous. The ultraviolet is produced inside the tube and is absorbed by the coating on the inner surface, which gives out visible light. It is that visible light which leaves the lamp and lights the room; the coating and the glass stop almost all the ultraviolet getting out.
items.random_wrong: Ultraviolet, which is the purple light that the human eye can see.

items.q: Why does a day spent outdoors in the Sun leave a person with a suntan?
items.correct: Ultraviolet from the Sun is absorbed by the skin and makes it darken.
items.misconception: Infrared from the Sun heats the skin, which turns it a darker colour.
items.why: Tanning happens on hot days and comes with the feeling of warmth, so the sensation of heat is taken to be the cause. Ultraviolet cannot be seen or felt, so it is easy to overlook. It is ultraviolet, not infrared, that tans the skin. Infrared is absorbed at the surface and simply warms it. Ultraviolet has a higher frequency, is ionising, and when absorbed changes cells in the skin so they produce more dark pigment – which is also why exposure raises the risk of skin cancer. Skin can tan on a cool, bright day and can burn in the shade.
items.random_wrong: Visible light is absorbed by the skin and adds colour to it.

items.q: An X-ray image of a hand shows the bones as light areas on a dark background. Why?
items.correct: Bone absorbs the X-rays, while soft tissue transmits them.
items.misconception: Bone transmits the X-rays, while soft tissue absorbs them.
items.why: Students remember that X-rays are penetrating and picture them punching through the hardest material of all, and they read the light bones on the image as ‘where the X-rays got through’ rather than ‘where they did not’. Dense material absorbs X-rays; soft tissue lets most of them pass. The detector is darkened where X-rays reach it, so the shadow behind the bone stays light. The bright region on the image is exactly where the X-rays were absorbed, which is why metal objects also appear light.
items.random_wrong: The X-rays reflect off the bone and back to the camera.

items.q: Gamma rays are used both for medical imaging and for treatment. Which use is described correctly?
items.correct: A beam of gamma rays is aimed at a tumour to destroy cancer cells.
items.misconception: Gamma rays are never aimed at a patient, as they only cause harm.
items.why: Teaching about the hazards of ionising radiation is emphatic, and students carry away a single rule – ionising means harmful – without the idea that a controlled dose aimed at the right place can do more good than harm. The hazard is real and doses are kept as low as possible, but that is a reason for care, not a reason never to use them. Imaging uses a small dose to gain information that could not be obtained without surgery. In treatment the ionising effect is the point: a beam is aimed at the tumour so that the cancer cells receive a high dose and the surrounding tissue receives much less.
items.random_wrong: Gamma rays are shone in and reflect off a tumour to image it.

items.q: A house sits in a valley with a hill between it and the transmitter, yet the radio still receives a clear signal. Why?
items.correct: Radio waves have long wavelengths, so they spread around the hill.
items.misconception: Radio waves travel faster than the other waves, so they get past it.
items.why: ‘Long wave’, ‘fast’ and ‘strong’ get blurred into one idea of a better wave, and the fact that broadcasts arrive instantly suggests exceptional speed rather than an ordinary property of all electromagnetic waves. All electromagnetic waves travel at the same speed through a vacuum, so speed cannot be the reason for choosing one part of the spectrum. Radio waves are chosen because their long wavelength lets them spread around hills and buildings, they are not strongly absorbed by the atmosphere, and they are not ionising, so broadcasting them over populated areas is safe.
items.random_wrong: Radio waves are the most penetrating of all, so they pass through it.

items.q: Why are microwaves, rather than long-wavelength radio waves, used to communicate with satellites?
items.correct: Microwaves pass through the atmosphere, while long radio waves are reflected.
items.misconception: Microwaves are reflected upwards by the atmosphere onto the satellite.
items.why: Students meet the idea that the ionosphere reflects radio waves and apply it to every transmitted signal, so reflection becomes the general way that signals get anywhere. Reflection by the ionosphere is what long-wavelength radio waves do, and it is precisely why they cannot be used for satellite links. Microwaves are chosen because they are transmitted through the atmosphere and the ionosphere, so a beam sent up from a dish reaches the satellite and the reply reaches the ground.
items.random_wrong: Microwaves travel faster than radio waves, so they reach orbit sooner.

items.q: Why can a microwave oven heat a thick piece of food faster than a grill can?
items.correct: Microwaves are absorbed by water a few centimetres into the food.
items.misconception: Microwaves are absorbed at the centre, so the middle heats first.
items.why: The phrase ‘cooks from the inside out’ is repeated so often that students take it literally. It also seems to explain why microwaved food can be hot in the middle and cool at the edges – which is really uneven absorption and uneven spreading of energy. Microwaves are absorbed as they enter the food, mainly in the outer few centimetres, and energy then spreads inwards by conduction. A microwave oven heats a thick piece of food faster than a grill does because energy is delivered throughout that outer layer rather than only to the surface, not because it starts in the centre.
items.random_wrong: Microwaves are infrared, which hot food absorbs very strongly.

items.q: Why does an electric bar heater warm a person standing in front of it in a cold room?
items.correct: Infrared travels straight to the person and is absorbed by their skin.
items.misconception: Infrared heats up the air first, and the warm air then heats the person.
items.why: Convection is the mechanism students meet most often for heating a room, and the air near a heater really is warmed, so it is taken to be the only route by which energy arrives. Infrared radiation travels directly from the heater to whatever is in front of it and is absorbed by that surface, which is why the warmth is felt at once and stops the instant something blocks the path. The air is warmed too, but the radiation does not need the air – it would cross a vacuum just as well.
items.random_wrong: The heater emits microwaves, which are absorbed inside the body.

items.q: A fibre optic cable bends round corners inside a building, yet the signal arrives undamaged. Which statement explains this?
items.correct: The light reflects from the walls of the fibre, so it stays inside.
items.misconception: The cable has straight sections joined by tiny mirrors at each bend.
items.why: ‘Light travels in straight lines’ is taught early and firmly, and students meet no everyday object in which light is made to follow a curved path, so a bent light path looks impossible. The light does travel in straight lines between reflections. Each time it meets the wall of the fibre at a shallow angle it is reflected back into the fibre, so a series of straight paths carries it round a gentle bend. Nothing is added at the corners, and because pure glass absorbs visible light so weakly the signal stays strong over long distances.
items.random_wrong: The signal is really a microwave signal, which bends round corners.

items.q: Why does producing ultraviolet inside a fluorescent lamp make the lamp energy efficient?
items.correct: A coating turns the ultraviolet into visible light, so little is wasted.
items.misconception: The ultraviolet leaves the lamp and lights the room without heating.
items.why: The specification pairs ultraviolet with energy efficient lamps, so students reasonably assume the ultraviolet is what leaves the lamp. Warnings about ultraviolet then make the lamp sound dangerous. The ultraviolet is produced inside the tube and is absorbed by the coating on the inner surface, which gives out visible light. It is that visible light which leaves the lamp and lights the room; the coating and the glass stop almost all the ultraviolet getting out.
items.random_wrong: Ultraviolet is brighter than light, so less of it is needed to see.

items.q: Why are gamma rays, rather than visible light, used to detect a tracer inside a patient's body?
items.correct: Gamma rays are penetrating, so they pass out of the body to a detector.
items.misconception: Gamma rays reflect off the tracer and form a picture on a film.
items.why: ‘Taking an X-ray’ sounds like taking a photograph, and everyday images are formed by reflected light, so reflection is assumed here too. Nothing is reflected back to a camera. The source is on one side of the patient and the detector on the other; bone absorbs the X-rays and soft tissue transmits them, so the image is a shadow. Gamma imaging works the other way round again: the tracer inside the patient emits the gamma rays, which pass out of the body to a detector.
items.random_wrong: Gamma rays are harmless, so any dose at all may be used safely.

items.q: Why can X-rays and gamma rays be used to treat a tumour deep inside the body?
items.correct: They penetrate the tissue and their ionising effect kills the cells.
items.misconception: They are safe at any dose at all, so a large beam can be aimed anywhere.
items.why: Teaching about the hazards of ionising radiation is emphatic, and students carry away a single rule – ionising means harmful – without the idea that a controlled dose aimed at the right place can do more good than harm. The hazard is real and doses are kept as low as possible, but that is a reason for care, not a reason never to use them. Imaging uses a small dose to gain information that could not be obtained without surgery. In treatment the ionising effect is the point: a beam is aimed at the tumour so that the cancer cells receive a high dose and the surrounding tissue receives much less.
items.random_wrong: They have longer wavelengths, which carry energy deep into the tissue.

items.q: What is a broadband signal made of as it travels along a fibre optic cable?
items.correct: Pulses of visible light.
items.misconception: It is a microwave or radio signal, the same as wi-fi – all modern communication is done with those waves.
items.why: Home internet is met mainly as a wireless service, and the word ‘broadband’ is attached to both the cable and the wi-fi in the house, so the two are treated as one technology. The specification pairs fibre optic communications with visible light. The signal travels along a thin glass fibre as pulses of light, reflected from the walls of the fibre so that it stays inside. Microwaves and radio waves travel through the air to an aerial or dish; they are not what carries the signal down the fibre.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A television is switched over using an infrared remote control. Does the programme also arrive as infrared?
items.correct: No. The programme is broadcast as radio waves; only the remote control uses infrared.
items.misconception: The television works on infrared, because that is the wave the remote control sends to it.
items.why: The one invisible signal a student has seen described for a television is the remote control’s infrared, so it becomes the wave associated with televisions in general. Two different applications are involved. Infrared travels a few metres from the handset to the television. The programme itself is broadcast as radio waves from a transmitter, which is the application the specification lists, and it is picked up by the aerial.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are infrared and microwaves the same kind of wave?
items.correct: No. They are different parts of the electromagnetic spectrum, with microwaves having the longer wavelength.
items.misconception: They are two names for the same waves – the ones that heat things up when they are absorbed.
items.why: Both are invisible, both are met almost entirely through appliances that heat food, and the spectrum diagram places them next to each other, so the distinction collapses. They are neighbouring groups in the spectrum but they are used differently because they behave differently. Microwaves are absorbed by water and penetrate a few centimetres into food, and they pass through the atmosphere, which is why they suit satellite links. Infrared is absorbed at the surface of an object, which is why it suits grills, heaters and thermal cameras.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Can ultraviolet be seen?
items.correct: No. Ultraviolet lies beyond the violet end of the visible spectrum, so the eye does not detect it.
items.misconception: Ultraviolet is the purple light you see coming out of a UV lamp at a bowling alley or a disco.
items.why: Lamps sold as ‘UV lamps’ do glow purple, and things fluoresce brightly under them, so the visible purple glow is taken to be the ultraviolet itself. The purple glow is visible light that the lamp also emits, and the bright colours are visible light given out by objects that absorb the ultraviolet. The ultraviolet itself is invisible. That is exactly the effect used in an energy efficient lamp, where a coating absorbs ultraviolet and gives out visible light.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Radio waves get past a hill and gamma rays get through a body. Is that the same property?
items.correct: No. Spreading around a large obstacle depends on a long wavelength; passing through matter depends on high frequency and energy.
items.misconception: It is all one thing – how strong the wave is. A strong wave gets through anything, and a weak one gets stopped.
items.why: Students collapse several properties into a single scale of ‘strength’ because both examples end with the signal arriving. Nothing in everyday language separates spreading around an obstacle from penetrating it. The two are opposite ends of the spectrum. Radio waves have the longest wavelengths and the lowest frequencies; they spread around hills and buildings but are readily blocked by matter. Gamma rays have the shortest wavelengths and the highest frequencies, carry the most energy and are ionising; they travel in straight lines and pass through matter. A wave cannot be good at both for the same reason.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.6.2.4 Uses and applications of electromagnetic waves
